Thorne vs Pure Encapsulations multivitamins, side by side — Not established: no source supported what this rests on.
This compares each brand's flagship once-daily multivitamin: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day and Pure Encapsulations O.N.E. Multivitamin. Each brand sells other multivitamins that are not covered here. I found no winner-neutral lab comparison of the two, so this rests on label data repeated by retailers and on the brands' own descriptions. Dosing. - Thorne's serving is two capsules. Only indicated, not established: A container holds 30 servings. [1] [2] Only indicated, not established: - Pure's serving is one capsule, taken daily with a meal. [29] [4] [30] [31] [5] Formulation. - Both supply vitamin D3 at 50 mcg. Only indicated, not established: Both supply folate as L-5-MTHF at 667 mcg DFE. [1] [3] [2] [29] [4] [30] [31] [5] - Thorne uses bisglycinate chelated minerals. Only indicated, not established: It has vitamin C 250 mg, high-dose B vitamins and both K1 and K2 at 200 mcg each. [1] [3] [2] - Pure's zinc is 25 mg as zinc citrate, and its vitamin C is 180 mg (the cited sources do not show: 25 mg). Only indicated, not established: It adds CoQ10 50 mg, alpha-lipoic acid 50 mg, and lutein, zeaxanthin and lycopene. [29] [4] [30] [31] [5] Only indicated, not established: - Pure's B-vitamin doses are much lower than Thorne's. Thiamin is 3 mg against 50 mg. [1] [3] [2] [29] [4] [30] [31] [5] Testing and certification. Only indicated, not established: - Thorne's Basic Nutrients 2/Day is labeled NSF Certified for Sport. [1] [6] - Pure says its products get additional testing by accredited, cGMP-certified laboratories (the cited sources do not show: cGMP-certified). Only indicated, not established: Its retailer listings carry a "third party tested" badge. [7] [8] [9] [10] - One third-party site says the O.N.E. Multivitamin is not NSF Certified for Sport. Only indicated, not established: That comes from a secondary source. [7] [8] [9] [10] - Another aggregator says it could not verify product-specific testing for the O.N.E. Only indicated, not established: Multivitamin. [7] [8] [9] [10] Price. Only indicated, not established: - Reported prices vary by seller and bottle size, and I did not confirm either product's current price. [10] [9] [11] - One comparison site reports a lower cost per serving for Pure's one-capsule product. Only indicated, not established: Its figures were $0.65 for Pure and $1.40 for Thorne. [10] [9] [11]
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day is a two-capsule serving, 30 servings per container, and carries an NSF Certified for Sport label.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne's formula per two capsules uses chelated minerals, L-5-MTHF folate at 667 mcg DFE, methylcobalamin B12 at 600 mcg, D3 at 50 mcg, vitamin C 250 mg, zinc 15 mg, thiamin 50 mg, B6 20 mg, and K1 and K2 (MK-4) at 200 mcg each.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Pure's O.N.E. is a one-capsule daily serving, taken with a meal. Its label shows D3 50 mcg, vitamin C 180 mg, zinc citrate 25 mg, thiamin 3 mg, B6 4 mg, Metafolin L-5-MTHF folate 667 mcg DFE, methylcobalamin B12 500 mcg, plus CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid and lutein.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne markets this product as NSF Certified for Sport.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Pure states that its products undergo third-party or accredited laboratory testing. I found no confirmation that O.N.E. carries NSF Certified for Sport.

What I couldn't establish
- Current official prices for both products. I searched retailer listings, but they conflict and none came from the brands. — No source covered it.
- Independent lab or ConsumerLab-type results for these two multivitamins. I found none in the results. — No source covered it.
- Pure's own certification page for the O.N.E. Multivitamin. I found only its brand description and retailer badges. — No source covered it.
- c1, Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day serving size, count per container and NSF Certified for Sport label — I ran no new search for it in this call. The held pages show no date, so when the label applied is unknown. It needs a check of the live Thorne page.
- c2, Thorne formula amounts — I ran no new search for it in this call. The held pages are undated and the live label was not checked.
- c3, O.N.E. label — the retailer pages I checked agree with the claim, but none states a date for the formula. I could not confirm the current label against Pure's own page.
- c4, Thorne's NSF Certified for Sport marketing — not re-searched in this call. The held pages are undated, and NSF's own certified-product listing was not checked.
- c5, Pure's testing statement and O.N.E. not carrying NSF Certified for Sport — the one search this call returned only retailer listings. They did not mention NSF Certified for Sport for O.N.E. That absence only shows I found no confirmation. It does not show the product lacks the certification. NSF's own listing would settle it.

Iron-free multivitamin pick: Thorne 2/Day or Pure O.N.E — Partly answered: 6 things it rests on aren't established.
Rests on findings that are not established: I'd pick Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day. Both products appear to be iron-free, so iron doesn't separate them. Only indicated, not established: Thorne's edge is its NSF Certified for Sport label. I found no confirmation that Pure's O.N.E. carries that label. The cost of choosing Thorne is two capsules a day instead of one. One caution applies to the Pure product. Pure also sells a separate "O.N.E. Only indicated, not established: Multivitamin with Iron" with 16 mg of iron per serving, so the label needs checking. My evidence for both iron-free claims comes from retailers and review sites. Only indicated, not established: I did not find either maker's own label page. [36] [11] [53] [35] [15] [37] [20] [38] [54] [55] [2] [41] [42] [39] [40]
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day contains no iron. The excerpts of Thorne's own page did not show its full supplement facts panel, so the claim still rests on secondary sources.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: The standard Pure O.N.E. Multivitamin contains no iron.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Pure sells a separate "O.N.E. Multivitamin with Iron" that contains 16 mg of iron per serving.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne markets Basic Nutrients 2/Day as NSF Certified for Sport. Some listings sell NSF and non-NSF versions of the product separately. The mindbodysoul page, for example, lists 120 capsules, 60 capsules, and 60 capsules NSF Certified for Sport. The certification appears to apply to the NSF-labelled version, and the buyer should check which one is in the cart.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: I found no confirmation that Pure O.N.E. carries NSF Certified for Sport. Pure says its products undergo third-party or accredited laboratory testing, which is a different claim. The product listings I read (Vitamin Shoppe, iHerb, PureFormulas and others) did not mention NSF Certified for Sport for O.N.E. Absence on those pages is not proof that it lacks the certification.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Pick Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day. Iron-free status does not separate the two, so the NSF Certified for Sport label is the tie-breaker.

Worth knowing
- Not shown by the cited sources: The Pure line includes an iron-containing sibling with a near-identical name. Not shown by the cited sources: Check that the bottle says "O.N.E. Only indicated, not established: Multivitamin" and not "with Iron" before buying. [39] [40]

What I couldn't establish
- Thorne's own label and Pure's own label, as proof of "no iron": the retailer and review pages I searched agree, but I did not find either maker's own page. — No source covered it.
- Whether Pure O.N.E. holds NSF Certified for Sport: no confirmation turned up in the pages I searched, and that is not the same as it lacking the certification. — No source covered it.
- Current first-party prices: not found; only retailer prices, which vary by seller and size. — No source covered it.
- Thorne's own supplement facts panel showing no iron (c1) — the one search returned Thorne's pages without the facts panel, so the iron-free status rests on secondary sources.
- Pure's own supplement facts for O.N.E., both the standard and with-iron versions (c2, c3) — not covered by this search. Earlier searches found only retailer and review pages.
- Whether Pure O.N.E. holds NSF Certified for Sport (c5) — I found no confirmation, and absence from retailer pages does not show it lacks the certification. I did not check the NSF certified-products database.
- Dates for any of these facts — none of the pages states when its content applied.

Recommendation: Choose Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day.
Because: both appear iron-free, and only Thorne has a marketed NSF Certified for Sport label that I could find. [36] [11] [53] [35] [15] [37] [20] [38] [54] [55] [2]
Assumes: the person wants a general daily multivitamin, is fine taking two capsules, and doesn't need the extras in O.N.E. such as CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid and lutein. The standard O.N.E. is the one without iron, not the "with Iron" version.
Changes if: the price gap matters more than the certification. It would also change if one-capsule convenience matters more, or if the person wants the added CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid and lutein. Confirmation that O.N.E. holds the NSF label would remove Thorne's main advantage. So would a Thorne label showing iron.
